title: AI Won’t Fix American Education
excerpt: While AI may transform how students learn, it is unlikely to address underlying inequalities that shape educational achievement, argues Sonia Murrow.
content_html:
Every generation seems to find a new approach to fix American education. Today, it's artificial intelligence.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, investor Marc Andreessen, and a growing number of policymakers argue that generative AI will democratize education by giving every student a personalized tutor, writing coach, research assistant, and study partner available around the clock. If every child has access to individualized instruction, they suggest, longstanding achievement gaps will begin to narrow.

It's an appealing vision. It is also a familiar one.

As a historian of education and former public school teacher, I have spent more than 35 years watching education reforms arrive with extraordinary fanfare and confidence. Each was promised to transform opportunities for disadvantaged students. Each produced some genuine benefits. Yet none fundamentally changed the inequalities that shape educational achievement in the U.S.

That is because Americans have long asked schools to solve problems that originate far beyond the classroom.

The belief itself is almost as old as public education. In 1848, Horace Mann, the first secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education, called schools "the great equalizer of the conditions of men." He believed education could prepare informed citizens while expanding opportunity for all. Nearly two centuries later, that ideal still shapes how Americans think about solving inequality. 

When gaps in achievement persist, we rarely ask whether schools alone can overcome them. Instead, we look for the next educational breakthrough.

During the 1990s and 2000s, that breakthrough was charter schools. Advocates argued that competition and innovation would dramatically improve outcomes for students in poor and underserved communities. Some charter schools did. Many did not. A 2023 Stanford University study found modest academic gains overall, but nothing approaching the transformation supporters had promised.

Around the same time, Teach For America offered another solution. By recruiting graduates from elite universities to teach in under-resourced schools, it hoped elite, young teachers could overcome educational disadvantage. Many participants became talented educators. But high turnover limited the program's reach, and no teaching corps—however committed—could erase the effects of poverty, housing instability, or unequal access to opportunity.

Then came No Child Left Behind. Signed into law in 2002, it promised that standards, testing, and accountability would finally close gaps in student achievement across race and class. The law succeeded in exposing disparities, but it also encouraged teaching to the test and narrowed what many schools taught. The gaps it sought to eliminate largely remained.

Now AI has become the latest reform wrapped in transformational promises. Its advocates are right about some of its potential in education. Generative AI can help explain difficult concepts, provide immediate feedback, translate instructional materials, and make individualized support more accessible than ever before. Teachers can use it to differentiate instruction and reduce routine administrative work. Used well, AI will almost certainly improve teaching and learning in many classrooms.

But what occurs in classrooms has never been the primary obstacle to educational equality. Students do not arrive at school with equal access to stable housing, nutritious food, quality health care, reliable internet, experienced teachers, safe neighborhoods, or family resources. These inequalities accumulate long before a child enters kindergarten and continue long after the school day ends. Chatbots, no matter how well-designed, will not erase them.

This is not an argument against AI, though we must pay close attention to both its real benefits and its real drawbacks, such as interfering with students' ability to think critically, which is no small thing. Schools should experiment with new technologies that genuinely help students learn.  As teachers have always adapted to new tools, from calculators to the internet, AI will almost certainly become another part of that evolution.

The problem arises when technological innovation is mistaken for social policy.

History suggests that educational reforms often aim to improve instruction without transforming the conditions that produce educational inequality in the first place. These reforms can make some schools better, some teachers more effective, and some students more successful. What they can’t do is eliminate the economic and social disparities that shape children's lives before they ever enter a classroom. Generative AI is unlikely to be different.

Americans continue to embrace Horace Mann's vision that public education expands opportunity. It goes without saying that schools matter enormously. They can ignite curiosity, inspire life goals, support critical relationships, and open doors to opportunities that might otherwise remain closed.

But schools have never been able to overcome inequality by themselves.

If we really want to narrow opportunity gaps, we must stop expecting educational innovations—whether charter schools, standardized testing, or artificial intelligence—to accomplish what only broader economic and social reforms can achieve.

AI may transform how students learn.

It will not, by itself, transform the unequal society that shapes students' lives and in which they learn.

content_html_zh:
每一代人似乎都找到了解决美国教育问题的新方法。 今天，它是人工智能。

微软首席执行官萨蒂亚·纳德拉 (Satya Nadella)、投资者马克·安德森 (Marc Andreessen) 和越来越多的政策制定者认为，生成式人工智能将为每个学生提供全天候的个性化导师、写作教练、研究助理和学习伙伴，从而实现教育民主化。 他们建议，如果每个孩子都能接受个性化指导，长期存在的成绩差距将开始缩小。

这是一个吸引人的愿景。 这也是一种熟悉的感觉。

作为一名教育史学家和前公立学校教师，我花了 35 年多的时间见证教育改革以非凡的宣传和信心到来。 每一项都承诺为弱势学生改变机会。 每一个都产生了一些真正的好处。 然而，这些都没有从根本上改变影响美国教育成就的不平等现象。

这是因为美国人长期以来一直要求学校解决远远超出课堂范围的问题。

这种信仰本身几乎与公共教育一样古老。 1848 年，马萨诸塞州教育委员会第一任秘书霍勒斯·曼 (Horace Mann) 称学校为“人类条件的伟大均衡器”。 他相信教育可以让公民做好知情的准备，同时为所有人增加机会。 近两个世纪后，这一理想仍然影响着美国人如何思考解决不平等问题。

当成绩差距持续存在时，我们很少问学校是否可以独自克服这些差距。 相反，我们寻找下一个教育突破。

20 世纪 90 年代和 2000 年代，特许学校取得了突破。 支持者认为，竞争和创新将极大地改善贫困和服务不足社区学生的学习成绩。 一些特许学校这样做了。 许多人没有。 斯坦福大学 2023 年的一项研究发现，整体学术进步不大，但远没有达到转型支持者所承诺的目标。

大约在同一时间，“为美国而教”提供了另一种解决方案。 通过招募精英大学毕业生到资源匮乏的学校任教，希望精英、年轻教师能够克服教育劣势。 许多参与者成为了才华横溢的教育家。 但人员流动率高限制了该计划的影响范围，而且任何教学团队——无论多么投入——都无法消除贫困、住房不稳定或机会不平等的影响。

然后是“不让一个孩子掉队”。 它于 2002 年签署成为法律，承诺标准、测试和问责制将最终缩小学生在种族和班级之间的成绩差距。 该法律成功地揭露了差异，但它也鼓励应试教育并缩小了许多学校的教学内容。 它试图消除的差距在很大程度上仍然存在。

现在，人工智能已成为包含变革承诺的最新改革。 它的倡导者关于它在教育方面的一些潜力是正确的。 生成式人工智能可以帮助解释困难的概念，提供即时反馈，翻译教学材料，并使个性化支持比以往任何时候都更容易获得。 教师可以用它来区分教学并减少日常行政工作。 如果使用得当，人工智能几乎肯定会改善许多课堂的教学。

但课堂上发生的事情从来都不是教育平等的主要障碍。 学生入学时并没有平等获得稳定的住房、营养食品、优质医疗保健、可靠的互联网、经验丰富的教师、安全的社区或家庭资源。 这些不平等现象在孩子进入幼儿园之前就已经积累起来，并在放学后持续很长时间。 聊天机器人，无论设计得多么好，都不会删除它们。

这并不是反对人工智能的论点，尽管我们必须密切关注它的真正好处和真正的缺点，例如干扰学生批判性思维的能力，这不是一件小事。 学校应该尝试真正帮助学生学习的新技术。 由于教师总是适应新工具，从计算器到互联网，人工智能几乎肯定会成为这一演变的另一部分。

当技术创新被误认为是社会政策时，问题就出现了。

历史表明，教育改革往往旨在改善教学，而不是首先改变造成教育不平等的条件。 这些改革可以使一些学校更好，一些教师更有效，一些学生更成功。 他们无法做到的是在孩子们进入课堂之前消除影响他们生活的经济和社会差异。 生成式人工智能不太可能有所不同。

美国人继续拥护霍勒斯·曼的公共教育扩大机会的愿景。 不言而喻，学校非常重要。 它们可以激发好奇心，激发人生目标，支持重要的关系，并为原本可能关闭的机会打开大门。

但学校始终无法独自克服不平等。

如果我们真的想缩小机会差距，我们就必须停止指望教育创新——无论是特许学校、标准化考试还是人工智能——来实现只有更广泛的经济和社会改革才能实现的目标。

人工智能可能会改变学生的学习方式。

它本身不会改变塑造学生生活和学习的不平等社会。
